name: Interview statistics, set 3
description: Statistics questions of the kind asked in online assessments and first rounds: pooled estimates, gamma updating, chi-squared counts, power, false discoveries, regression standard errors, half-lives and noise bands. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Two independent unbiased estimates of the same mean have variances 4 and 12. You combine them as a weighted average whose weights sum to 1.
items.question: What is the smallest variance such an average can have?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each estimate by the inverse of its variance.

byKey.equal-weights: You weighted the two equally, which gives (4 + 12)/4 = 4. Weight each estimate by the inverse of its variance instead.
byKey.average-variances: You averaged the two variances. Averaging the estimates also shrinks the variance, so the best average does better than either one.
byKey.total-precision: You stopped at the total precision, 1/4 + 1/12 = 1/3. The pooled variance is its reciprocal, 3.

explain.text: Weight each estimate by the inverse of its variance, so the weights are 3/4 and 1/4. The pooled variance is $1/(1/4 + 1/12) = 3$. No other weights that sum to 1 give less.

items.prose: You draw five values from a population with variance 10. You estimate the variance by summing the squared deviations from the sample mean and dividing by 5.
items.question: What is the expected value of your estimate?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the squared deviations from the sample mean sum to on average.

byKey.no-bias: You took the estimate as unbiased. Dividing by n rather than n - 1 shrinks it by the factor 4/5.
byKey.wrong-way: You multiplied by 5/4. That factor corrects the estimate; the estimate itself is 4/5 of 10.

explain.text: Squared deviations from the sample mean sum to $(n - 1)\sigma^2$ on average, not $n\sigma^2$. Dividing by n gives $\tfrac{4}{5} \times 10 = 8$. The estimate runs low by $\sigma^2/n$, which is 2 here.

items.prose: A 95% confidence interval for a mean runs from 2 to 10. It was built as the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors.
items.question: Using 2.576 as the 99% multiplier, what is the upper end of the 99% interval, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the centre and the half-width, then scale the half-width.

byKey.added-gap: You added the gap in multipliers, 0.616, to the end point. The half-width scales with the multiplier: it becomes 4 times 2.576/1.96.
byKey.scaled-end: You scaled the end point, 10, by 2.576/1.96. Scale the half-width of 4 about the centre of 6 instead.

explain.text: The centre is 6 and the half-width is 4, so one standard error is $4/1.96$. The 99% half-width is $4 \times 2.576/1.96 \approx 5.257$. The upper end is $6 + 5.257 = 11.257$, or 11.26.

items.prose: Orders arrive as a Poisson process. Your prior for the rate per day is a gamma distribution with shape 3 and rate 1. You then count 12 orders in 5 days.
items.question: What is the posterior mean of the rate per day, to 1 decimal place?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the count to the prior shape and the days to the prior rate.

byKey.data-only: You used the data alone, 12/5. The prior adds 3 to the count and 1 to the days.
byKey.prior-only: You gave the prior mean, 3/1. The 12 orders in 5 days pull it towards 2.4.

explain.text: A gamma prior with shape a and rate b acts like a events seen in b days. The posterior has shape $3 + 12 = 15$ and rate $1 + 5 = 6$. Its mean is $15/6 = 2.5$ a day.

items.prose: You roll a die 60 times. Faces 1 to 6 come up 5, 8, 9, 8, 10 and 20 times.
items.question: What is the chi-squared statistic against a fair die, to 1 decimal place?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square each gap from the expected count and divide by that count.

byKey.not-divided: You summed the squared gaps and stopped. Divide each by the expected count of 10.
byKey.absolute-gaps: You used the gaps themselves, not their squares. The statistic squares each gap before dividing by 10.

explain.text: Each face expects 10 rolls, so the squared gaps are 25, 4, 1, 4, 0 and 100. Their sum over the expected count is $134/10 = 13.4$. That beats 11.07, the 5% point on 5 degrees of freedom, so you reject a fair die.

items.prose: Over 400 trading days a signal earns a mean of 0.05% a day. Its daily standard deviation is 1%.
items.question: What is the t statistic of its mean daily return, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the mean by its standard error, not by the daily spread.

byKey.no-root: You divided the mean by the daily standard deviation and stopped. The standard error of the mean is 1% over the root of 400.
byKey.annual-sharpe: You scaled by the root of 252, which gives an annual Sharpe ratio. The t statistic uses the root of the 400 days.

explain.text: The standard error of the mean is 1% over $\sqrt{400} = 20$, which is 0.05%. So t is $0.05/0.05 = 1$. To reach t = 2 the same edge needs four times the data, 1,600 days.

items.prose: You want to detect a mean shift of 2 when the standard deviation is 10. The test is two-sided at 5%, using 1.96, and you want power of 80%, using 0.8416.
items.question: By the usual normal formula, what is the smallest sample size that gives this power?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two normal points, scale by the sd over the shift, square, and round up.

byKey.no-power: You used 1.96 alone, which gives only 50% power. Add 0.8416 for 80% power before squaring.
byKey.one-sided: You used 1.645, the one-sided point. The test is two-sided, so use 1.96.
byKey.rounded-down: You rounded 196.2 down. At 196 the power is 79.95%, just short, so round up.

explain.text: You need $\sqrt{n} \times 2/10$ to reach $1.96 + 0.8416 = 2.8016$, so $\sqrt{n} = 2.8016 \times 5 = 14.008$. Squared, that is about 196.2, so round up to 197. At 196 the power is 0.7995, just short of 80%.

items.prose: You test 200 independent signals, each at the 1% level, and 14 of them pass. Assume nearly all of the 200 have no real edge.
items.question: What share of the 14 passes do you expect to be false, in per cent to 1 decimal place?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the passes that luck alone would give, then compare with 14.

byKey.gave-level: You gave the test level, 1%. That is the chance a null signal passes, not the share of passes that are false.
byKey.pass-rate: You gave 14/200, the share of signals that passed. Compare the expected false passes with the 14 passes instead.

explain.text: If the signals have no edge, 1% of 200 pass by luck: 2 of them. So about 2 of the 14 passes, or $2/14 \approx 14.3\%$, are false. A few real signals among the 200 would make it slightly lower.

items.prose: A simple regression of y on x has total sum of squares 200 and residual sum of squares 50. The fitted slope is negative.
items.question: What is the correlation between x and y, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $R^2$ first, then take its root with the slope's sign.

byKey.sign: You dropped the sign. The correlation takes the sign of the slope, which is negative.
byKey.no-root: You gave $R^2$ itself. The correlation is its square root, with the slope's sign.
byKey.residual-share: You took the root of 50/200, the share left unexplained. Use 1 minus that share, 0.75.

explain.text: Here $R^2 = 1 - 50/200 = 0.75$. In a simple regression the correlation is the root of $R^2$, with the slope's sign. So $r = -\sqrt{0.75} \approx -0.866$.

items.prose: A straight line is fitted by least squares to 25 points, with residual standard deviation 2. You want to predict one new observation at the mean of x.
items.question: What is the standard error of that prediction, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the variance of the fitted line to the variance of a new point's noise.

byKey.fitted-mean: You gave the error of the fitted line at the mean, 2/5. A new observation also carries its own noise of sd 2.
byKey.noise-only: You gave the noise of the new point alone. The fitted line is itself estimated, which adds 4/25 to the variance.

explain.text: At the mean of x the fitted line has standard error $2/\sqrt{25} = 0.4$. A new point adds its own noise, so the variances add: $4 + 0.16 = 4.16$. The root is $\sqrt{4.16} \approx 2.04$.

items.prose: You fit a straight line by least squares. The line has the right shape, but the residuals spread wider as x grows.
items.question: What does the fanning do to the fit?

options.text: The slope stays unbiased, but its usual standard error is wrong.
The slope is biased upwards, but its usual standard error holds.
options.why: You blamed the slope. Uneven noise still averages out, so the slope is unbiased; the error formula is what fails.

options.text: Nothing changes, since least squares assumes nothing of the noise.
options.why: You took least squares to need no assumptions. Its usual standard error assumes the noise has one spread at every x.

options.text: The fitted $R^2$ can turn negative as the noise grows with x.
options.why: You expected $R^2$ below zero. With an intercept, least squares keeps $R^2$ between 0 and 1.

feedback.correct: Correct. The slope is fine on average; its reported error is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which part of the usual output assumes one noise variance.

explain.text: Least squares stays unbiased whatever the noise, but its usual standard error assumes one noise variance. With noise sd 0.2x and 50 points, slopes average 0.500 for a true 0.5. The reported error averages 0.057, against a true spread of 0.063.

items.prose: You want the coefficient on $x_1$ from the regression of y on both $x_1$ and $x_2$. You may only run regressions with one predictor.
items.question: Which recipe gives exactly that coefficient?

options.text: Regress y on $x_2$ and $x_1$ on $x_2$; regress residual on residual.
Regress y on $x_1$ alone and read off the slope that it gives.
options.why: You dropped $x_2$. When the two predictors are correlated, the simple slope also picks up the effect of $x_2$.

options.text: Regress y on $x_2$, then regress that residual on the raw $x_1$.
options.why: You cleaned y but not $x_1$. The part of $x_1$ that moves with $x_2$ must come out too.

options.text: Regress y on $x_1$ and on $x_2$ in turn; average the two slopes.
options.why: You averaged two simple slopes. Each mixes in the other predictor's effect, and averaging does not undo that.

feedback.correct: Correct. Partial $x_2$ out of both, then regress residual on residual.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is left of y and of $x_1$ once $x_2$ is taken out of each.

explain.text: This is the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell result: strip $x_2$ out of both y and $x_1$, then regress what is left. In a sample of 20,000 with true coefficient 2, the recipe and the full regression both give 1.981. The simple slope of y on $x_1$ gives 2.888.

items.prose: A spread's deviation from its mean follows an AR(1) process with coefficient 0.75 a day.
items.question: What is the half-life of a deviation in days, to 1 decimal place?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve for the k at which the coefficient to the power k is one half.

byKey.linear-decay: You divided 0.5 by 0.25, as if the deviation shrank by the same amount each day. It shrinks by the same factor, 0.75.
byKey.time-scale: You gave 1/(1 - 0.75), a rough time scale of reversion. The half-life solves $0.75^k = 0.5$.

explain.text: After k days a deviation keeps $0.75^k$ of its size. Set $0.75^k = 0.5$, so $k = \ln 0.5/\ln 0.75 \approx 2.41$ days. Two days leave 56% and three leave 42%.

items.prose: You have 400 observations of a series you believe is white noise, and you plot its sample autocorrelations.
items.question: What is the half-width of the usual 95% band around zero, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the standard error of one sample autocorrelation under white noise.

byKey.no-multiplier: You gave one standard error, 1/20. The 95% band is 1.96 standard errors wide on each side.
byKey.divided-by-n: You divided 1.96 by n. The standard error is one over the root of n, so divide by 20.

explain.text: Under white noise each sample autocorrelation has standard error about $1/\sqrt{400} = 0.05$. The 95% band is 1.96 of those on each side: $1.96/20 = 0.098$. A bar beyond 0.098 is unusual at the 5% level.

items.prose: A portfolio holds 25 assets in equal weights. Each asset has volatility 20%, and every pair of assets correlates 0.25.
items.question: What is the portfolio volatility, in per cent to 1 decimal place?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the variance into the own-variance part and the covariance part.

byKey.independent: You treated the assets as independent, 20% over the root of 25. The correlation of 0.25 keeps most of the risk.
byKey.many-asset-limit: You gave the limit for very many assets, 20% times the root of 0.25. With 25 assets the own-variance part still adds a little.

explain.text: With equal weights the variance is $\sigma^2(1/n + (1 - 1/n)\rho)$. Here that is $0.04 \times (0.04 + 0.96 \times 0.25) = 0.0112$. Its root is about 10.6%, just above the 10% floor that many assets would reach.
